en: The great beast Kulansur
They brought before Seytek,
Led by six strongmen.
A white halter tied in a round knot,
A halter fitted exactly to Kulansur;
They smoothed and secured his forelock,
And, lest a stray bullet strike him,
They covered him with armor.
Lest, on a long and distant journey,
The sharpness of his hooves be worn away,
They shod him with shoes of steel.
Such was Kulansur’s nature;
This was the appearance
Of the restless dark steed.
For the champion who came from the fairies,
And for the many appointed lands,
All who saw him marveled.
His beauty surpassed that of every beast,
And he did not brush the heads of reeds.
When Kulansur gave chase,
He never failed to overtake a spirit-being.
He did not graze the tops of rushes;
When that spirited beast grew excited,
He never failed to catch a gazelle.
He did not touch the tips of dry stalks;
When that magnificent beast pursued,
He never failed to catch a wild ass.
His tail streamed like a parrot’s plume;
If a ninety-fathom chasm appeared,
He leapt it without a pause.
Steel horseshoes fitted him perfectly;
His barrel was broad, his neck well-set.
“This is a steed of splendid build,”
My father Jelkayyp judged.
Look upon his foreleg bone:
It was like a stake hammered into the ground.
The breadth of his rounded croup
Was like a plateau atop a summer pasture.
His split hooves were like deep ravines,
His jaw like cast steel.
Prancing, kicking, and biting,
He allowed no stranger
To come near him.
When he trotted, he moved like a gazelle;
Stepping briskly and frisking,
When he set off, he moved like a fox.
His tail spread across his thighs;
He had been born for the fortune
Of the blessed gray-maned hero.
The peerless thoroughbred Kulansur—
Even the six grooms who tended him
Treated him as though he might bring them harm.
They held back in fear,
And the more they did, the more Kulansur
Flattened his ears like a tiger;
The restless creature
Struck and churned the earth.
Three heroes among the strongmen
Gripped his bridle firmly
And turned his neck toward the hitching post.
Another hero made ready
And prepared the saddlecloth.
The heroes spread out
The leather saddle blanket
And saddled Kulansur.
The front bow was solid gold,
The rear bow solid silver;
The golden saddle shone like the moon on his brow,
With jewels set into its bow,
As though lighting a lantern for all who saw.
The white saddle was perfectly made,
And fitted Kulansur exactly.
They tightened the breast strap firmly,
And left the rear girth loose,
For he would travel down slopes
And enter descending ground.
The eager warriors
Shortened the crupper.
It was clear he was the lion among lions;
As he pulled straight ahead,
The hero thrust his feet into
The gold-soled stirrups and sprang astride.
The hearts of all who saw were stirred;
That imposing, beloved hero
Looked like a lofty blue mountain.
“Saddle up quickly!” he cried,
Hurrying his lions.
He made Kulansur, built like a wild ram,
Stride out at a proud, swinging pace.
Rumbling and gathering force,
He spoke softly to himself;
At twilight his eyes were like mist,
His chest like that of a fearsome tiger.
Speaking firmly after taking stock,
He addressed the noble heroes.
“O muraas inscribed upon my brow by fate,
All of you lion-hearted champions,
Have you seen what I have seen,
And learned what I have learned?
Yesterday, when I sent Akjoltoy ahead,
He was worth a host against the shooting foe.
Wearing out horses and surveying the land,
Loosing hounds and flying hunting birds,
My khan-uncle went out scouting;
It seems he camped briefly at the ford.
It seems his destined road lay there,
And that he knew well the path of campaigning.
It seems it was a tiger’s road;
My uncle was a true man, his spirit stirred,
And it seems countless paths opened before him.
Encountering the sacred Night of Power,
He found what he desired,
And my blessed uncle
Found a black-eyed beauty.
Will not the thoroughbreds turn their heads?
Will the warriors not ride without rest
Until they reach my blessed uncle?”
Thus spoke Seytek the panther:
“Today let us cross a month’s journey,
And loosen the reins of our horses.
Let the cherished thoroughbreds’
Rumps ripple like those of wild rams,
And their backs straighten like argali.
Let the dust rise and divide the sky;
Today let their pedigree be revealed.
Let this restless heart be calmed,
And the thoroughbreds’ eyes be opened.
Let the black stones struck by their hooves
Fly apart like sparks from flint.
Let the ringing beneath their feet
Shoot into the sky like arrows.
I burn with wrath and long to see her;
Akbermet is the one I desire.
I lose all peace and yearn to see her;
Akbermet is the one I seek.
My young living heart is torn apart,
And one night seems like a thousand to me.
The reason she is about to appear is this:
Stricken by the pain she chose to face,
I heard that Akbermet is coming.
My dear uncle,
I heard this news from Akjoltoy.
I heard she scattered all her countless riches
And left them behind
To the fairy who served her.
I heard she gathered a company of fairies
And, leaving her ruined realm,
Is leading them here.
I heard her words remained:
She lamented and cried,
‘Oh, Seytek!’ in bitter longing.
I heard she burned her champion in the flames,
While she herself remained.
I heard she arrayed
Her gold and precious jewels.
I heard Akbermet voiced her sorrow,
Lamenting to God,
And saying, ‘Seytek, my betrothed,’
Set out to search for me.
I heard the unfortunate queen
Was reduced to misery.
I heard that for Seytek
Her dear head languished in yearning.
She set forth upon a journey,
Crossing many deserts along the way,
Passing frozen, looming mountains,
And descending through deep ravines,
Crying out in anguish to the Creator.
‘We have seen what we longed to see while still alive,’ she says,
‘The one I desired has come,’ she says.
I am dying in the flames of love,
And my thoughts scatter in countless directions.
For that unfortunate one who has suffered,
For the beloved daughter of the fairies,
My dear lions,
“What can I do for him?”—
So saying, he grew impassioned,
And spoke aloud to the empty world;
The noble warrior hastened toward his beloved,
The poor warrior rushed on anxiously.
Over the lofty Akjoltoy Pass,
And through valleys broad and deep,
Lion-hearted Seytek, the leopard,
The noble hero who took after his father,
Never turned Kulansur’s head aside,
Nor paused to yearn for his beloved.
He followed the length of Keng-Özön,
Watching the trail of Kulunsur.
Hero Seytek rode in front,
Driving fiercely across the hills,
Having covered the courser beneath him
With a fine silk horsecloth.
They took the well-trodden road,
Following the pale trail of Joltoy,
Who had departed on his journey,
And joyfully took the road,
Following the dusty tracks
Of worthy Joltoy, heir to the legacy.
They traced their way along the valley,
Having shod every one
Of the many steeds with steel.
Whenever the chance arose, they raced;
The many steeds flew like clouds,
Straining neck and neck.
In some places the coursers
Stretched their strides beyond all measure,
As though despairing of their borrowed lives,
As though about to plunge into an abyss.
Whenever they reached open ground,
They darted like flying birds,
And drawing straight toward the distant phantom,
They pursued and drew near.
Whenever they came to another stretch,
Their dust whirled like a whirlwind;
The coursers, now in their prime,
Whistled onward like arrows from a bow.
When their hooves struck stone,
Sparks scattered like millet.
Their qualities as thoroughbreds showed plainly,
And wherever their hooves struck,
The ground split like a riverbank.
The restless heroes raced,
Their stirrups clashing;
The coursers, now in full form,
Pulled so hard their riders’ arms grew numb.
Kulansur, leading before them,
Thrummed like a drawn bowstring,
Roaring onward like a flying cloud.
Now he appeared in sight,
And when the wretch vanished,
He dissolved into blue smoke.
His cavernous mouth gaped wide,
And dust sprayed from the earth;
Every living creature
Was overwhelmed by his thunder.
His stride opened wide as an argali’s,
And the grey wolf riding upon him
Opened his eyes as wide as bowls,
Saying, “What a matchless courser!”
His aching desire was soothed;
When his steed flew like a cloud,
The grey wolf’s spirit brightened.
His heart surged and he lost himself,
And through the hero’s mind
A thousand different thoughts passed:
“To ride forth and take vengeance on the foe—
That is the custom left by my forefathers.
Well done, Kulansur!
With sovereign God as my ally,
You are my wing descended from the fairies.
Though I travel a distant road for six months,
I shall fly like a shimmering mirage.
Whatever deed I pray to accomplish,
I shall attain my desire.
My iron-hoofed courser never tires
When ranging far on reconnaissance.
